# Adapt plot_mixture_v4's histogram without evaluating a fitted model.
# Retain paper weights, bin width and empirical handling of censored values.
plot_histogram <- function(dataset, title = NULL, xmax = 10) {
  dt <- paper_data %>% filter(.data$dataset == .env$dataset) %>%
    calc_study_weights()
  exact_z <- abs(dt$z[dt$z_operator == "="])
  exact_z <- exact_z[!is.na(exact_z)]
  prepared <- prepare_mixture_z(dt$z, dt$z_operator)
  dt$z <- prepared$z
  dt$z_operator <- prepared$operator
  dt <- resample_inequalities_for_hist(dt, exact_z)
  ggplot(dt, aes(x = abs(z), y = after_stat(density), weight = weights)) +
    geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 25.235, by = 0.245),
                   fill = "#377EB8", alpha = 0.30, colour = NA) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1.96, linetype = "dotted",
               colour = "#6B7280", linewidth = 0.4) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, xmax), ylim = c(0, 0.7), expand = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1.96, 4, 6, 8, 10),
                       labels = c("0", "1.96", "4", "6", "8", "10")) +
    labs(x = expression(abs(z)), y = "Density", title = title) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 17, base_family = plot_font) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, colour = "#174C70"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#E6E7E9", linewidth = 0.3),
          panel.border = element_rect(colour = "#BFC4C8", linewidth = 0.3))
}

## Studying the quality of empirical science

- The replication crisis refuted the intuition that a significance threshold
  can tell us whether a study is good.
- Even $p<0.01$ versus $p>0.2$ does not discriminate well between high and
  low signal-to-noise ratios (SNR = effect size / SE).
- Many people remain dismayed when results "fail to replicate", despite
  knowing that we should not rely on a single study.
- Can we reconcile these problems with a more positive view of
  statistically based science?

\vfill
\slidesource{Two-sided $p$-values of 0.01 and 0.2 correspond to $|z|=2.58$
and $1.28$. These are about equally likely at a signal-to-noise ratio of
$(2.58+1.28)/2=1.93$, which corresponds to 49\% power.}

## Ioannidis 2005: binary model of scientific findings

Research findings are compared against "true relationships" and
"no relationships" in a scientific field.

\vspace{0.15cm}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{l|c|c}
 & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Ground Truth}} \\
 & No relationship & True relationship \\
\hline
Significant & False positive & True positive \\
\hline
Non-significant & True negative & False negative \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}


$$\begin{array}{lll}
\text{Null studies:} & \mathrm{SNR}=0 & \mathrm{PoS}=0.05 \\
\text{Non-null studies, e.g.:} & |\mathrm{SNR}|=2.8 & \mathrm{PoS}\approx0.80
\end{array}$$

- Low TR/NR ratio = most published findings are false = low replication rate

\vfill
\slidesource{Ioannidis (2005). \textit{Why Most Published Research Findings Are False}. PLoS Medicine 2(8): e124.}

## Limitations of the $2 \times 2$ model

**1. The goal is not to separate "no relationships" from "true relationships".**

Effects of interest are rarely exactly zero. With finite data, it is not
possible to distinguish effects that are zero from those that are small.

\vspace{0.2cm}

**2. The binary model is not a realistic representation of empirical research.**

In particular, assumption of some fixed power for TR's. Researchers do not know the true 
effect when designing a study. SNRs are on a continuum.

## Two contributions of this paper

**Data: Benchmarks of Empirical Accuracy in Research (BEAR)**

- We make a large number of results from empirical research easily accessible.
- We process the available data to make them ready for metascientific research,
  with clear documentation and open-source code.

\vspace{0.4cm}

**Method: a model of empirical $z$-values and signal-to-noise ratios**

- Extend existing models to accommodate selective reporting and truncation.
- Estimate main metascientific characteristics of fields of research
  (power, sign, replication).

\vfill
\slidesource{Stephens (2017), \textit{False discovery rates: a new deal}; van Zwet et al. (2021), \textit{The statistical properties of RCTs and a proposal for shrinkage}; van Zwet and Gelman (2022), \textit{A proposal for informative default priors scaled by the standard error of estimates}.}

## BEAR

**Benchmarks of Empirical Accuracy in Research**

24 datasets · 12.5 million results · 7,476 meta-analyses

- Existing meta-analyses, systematic reviews, trial registries,
  metascience datasets and replication projects.
    - Side note: better databases of *replications* elsewhere.
- This paper: 16 corpora, `r comma(sum(corpus_table$results))` results
  from `r comma(sum(corpus_table$study_units))` studies.
- Medicine, economics, psychology, psychotherapy, ecology and evolution,
  political science, education, and other fields.
- We do not contribute any new data; all data collection and the vast
  majority of processing were done by the creators of the source datasets.

## $z$-values and signal-to-noise ratios

\small

For study $i$, true effect $\beta_i$ and estimate $\hat\beta_i$:

$$
z_i = \frac{\hat\beta_i}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_i)}, \qquad
\mathrm{SNR}_i = \frac{\beta_i}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_i)}.
$$

Suppose that we have unbiased effect estimates which are normally distributed
with known standard errors. Then

$$
z_i = \mathrm{SNR}_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim N(0,1),
$$

where the error is independent of the SNR.

\vspace{0.2cm}

For two-sided $p$-values:

$$p=0.05 \Rightarrow |z|=1.96,\quad
p=0.01 \Rightarrow |z|=2.58,\quad
p=0.001 \Rightarrow |z|=3.29.$$




## A model for the distribution of $z$-values

Our main assumption is that the distribution of the absolute $z$-values is
well represented by a **mixture of half-normal distributions**.

Equivalently, we model signed $z$-values as a mixture of zero-mean normals:

$$
f(z\mid p,\sigma)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i\,\frac{1}{\sigma_i}
\phi\!\left(\frac{z}{\sigma_i}\right).
$$

- $\phi$ is the standard normal density.
- $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_k)$: non-negative mixture weights that sum to unity.
- $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k)$: standard deviations, at least 1
  because every $z$-value has a standard normal noise component.
- We use $k=4$. No need to go higher, could go lower in most cases.



## From signal-to-noise ratios to $z$-values

The $z$-value is equal to the SNR plus an independent standard normal error.

```{r convolution, fig.width=11.5, fig.height=3, out.width='97%'}
# Illustrative convolution, before publication selection; not an empirical fit.
x <- seq(-7, 7, length.out = 701)
illustration <- tibble(
  x, `SNR` = 0.7 * dnorm(x, sd = 0.6) + 0.3 * dnorm(x, sd = 2.5),
  `Independent error: N(0,1)` = dnorm(x),
  `Observed z = SNR + error` =
    0.7 * dnorm(x, sd = sqrt(0.6^2 + 1)) +
    0.3 * dnorm(x, sd = sqrt(2.5^2 + 1))
) %>% pivot_longer(-x, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density")
illustration$distribution <- factor(illustration$distribution,
  levels = c("SNR", "Independent error: N(0,1)", "Observed z = SNR + error"))
ggplot(illustration, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#377EB8", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = "#174C70", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ distribution, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-6, 0, 6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 15, base_family = plot_font) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(colour = "#174C70"))
```





## Deconvolution: the distribution of the SNRs

The distribution of the $z$-values is a convolution of the distribution of
the SNRs and the standard normal error:

$$z=\mathrm{SNR}+\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,1).$$

\vspace{0.35cm}

We simply **subtract 1 from the variances of the mixture components**:

$$
f_{\mathrm{SNR}}(x\mid p,\sigma)
= f\!\left(x\mid p,\sqrt{\sigma^2-1}\right).
$$

\vspace{0.2cm}

Component $i$ has variance $\sigma_i^2$ for $z$ and $\sigma_i^2-1$ for SNR.

## Adjustment for selective reporting

\small

Following Hedges, define $\omega$ as the relative risk that a result with
$|z|<1.96$ is observed compared to a result with $|z|\geq1.96$:

$$\omega=
\frac{\Pr(\text{result is published}\mid |z|<1.96)}
{\Pr(\text{result is published}\mid |z|\geq1.96)}.$$

The density conditional on publication becomes

$$f(z\mid p,\sigma,\omega,\mathrm{pub})=
\begin{cases}
\omega\,f(z\mid p,\sigma)/C(p,\sigma,\omega), & |z|<1.96,\\[3pt]
f(z\mid p,\sigma)/C(p,\sigma,\omega), & |z|\geq1.96.
\end{cases}$$

The normalising constant is

$$C(p,\sigma,\omega)=\omega\Pr(|z|<1.96\mid p,\sigma)
+\Pr(|z|\geq1.96\mid p,\sigma).$$

\vfill
\slidesource{Hedges (1984, 1992). “pub” denotes conditioning on publication.}

## Truncation, repeated estimates, and likelihood

\small
\setlength{\abovedisplayskip}{4pt}
\setlength{\belowdisplayskip}{4pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{3pt}

**Reported values are sometimes truncated.**

- Statements such as $p<0.05$, $p<0.01$, or $p<0.001$ give bounds on $|z|$.
- $\tilde z$ denotes the possibly censored value; $\delta$ indicates
  left censoring, right censoring, or no censoring.

**Most datasets have multiple $z$-values per study.**

- To prevent studies with many $z$-values from dominating the likelihood,
  weight observations by the inverse number of $z$-values per study.

For $n$ observations, we maximise the weighted log likelihood

$$\ell(p,\sigma,\omega)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_j
\log f(\tilde z_j,\delta_j\mid p,\sigma,\omega,\mathrm{pub}),$$

Here $w_j$ is the weight of observation $j$.

\vfill

## Quantities implied by the distribution of the SNRs

\small

**Probability of significance**

$$\mathrm{PoS}(\mathrm{SNR})=\mathrm{PoS}(|\mathrm{SNR}|)
=\Pr(|z|\geq1.96\mid\mathrm{SNR}).$$

Averaging over the distribution of the SNR gives the **assurance**,
$\overline{\mathrm{PoS}}$.

**Conditional probability of the correct sign**

$$\Pr(z\cdot\mathrm{SNR}>0\mid |z|).$$

**Conditional probability of "successful replication"**

$$\Pr(z_{\mathrm{repl}}\cdot z>0\text{ and }|z_{\mathrm{repl}}|>1.96\mid |z|).$$

We imagine a second study with **exactly the same SNR**:
$z_{\mathrm{repl}}=\mathrm{SNR}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{repl}}$, with independent
$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{repl}}\sim N(0,1)$.

## Conditional inference for SNR given $z$

\small

The marginal distribution of $z$, together with the conditional distribution
of $z$ given SNR, determines the joint distribution.

The conditional distribution of **SNR given $z$** is a mixture of normals:

$$\mathrm{SNR}\mid z\ \sim\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}q_i(z)\,
N\!\left(\mu_i(z),\tau_i^2\right),$$

with weights, means, and variances

$$q_i(z)=\frac{p_i\phi(z/\sigma_i)/\sigma_i}{f(z\mid p,\sigma)},\qquad
\mu_i(z)=\frac{\sigma_i^2-1}{\sigma_i^2}\,z,\qquad
\tau_i^2=\frac{\sigma_i^2-1}{\sigma_i^2}.$$

For an exact replication, $z_{\mathrm{repl}}\mid z$ has the same weights
and means, with variances **$\tau_i^2+1$**.

\vfill

## Decreasing distributions of absolute $z$-values

```{r decreasing-panels, fig.width=11.5, fig.height=3, out.width='97%'}
# Reuse the trial-phase data and fits used in the paper's subset figure.
subgroup_fits <- readRDS(file.path(bear_root, "explore/subgroups/fits.rds"))
phase_panels <- subgroup_fits$manifest %>%
  filter(category == "Phase", subgroup %in% c("phase1", "phase2", "phase3")) %>%
  arrange(subgroup)
stopifnot(nrow(phase_panels) == 3)
set.seed(20260925)
wrap_plots(lapply(seq_len(nrow(phase_panels)), function(i) {
  key <- phase_panels$fit_name[i]
  plot_mixture_v4(subgroup_fits$fits[[key]], subgroup_fits$dfs[[key]],
    nm = paste("ClinicalTrials.gov — Phase", i), col = "#174C70",
    ymax = 0.4, annotate = "none", show_corrected = TRUE,
    align_corrected_above_threshold = TRUE, corrected_colour = "#555B61") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
    labs(x = "|z|", y = "Density") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 15, base_family = plot_font) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13, colour = "#174C70"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}), nrow = 1)
```

- Mixtures of half-normal densities are necessarily decreasing. But data support 
this strongly.
- The main difference between the distributions of the $z$-values is their
  **widths**. A wider distribution of $z$-values implies a wider distribution
  of SNRs.
- Since PoS is an increasing function of the absolute SNR, a higher
  proportion of results will reach statistical significance.


## What does the selection parameter tell us?

```{r results-setup, include=FALSE}
source(file.path(bear_root, "R/psr.R"))

# Reuse the displayed paper tables, rather than regenerate their estimates.
table_keys <- c(
  "Nuijten et al" = "Nuijten", "Askarov et al" = "Askarov",
  "Metapsy" = "Metapsy", "Arel-Bundock et al" = "ArelBundock",
  "Costello and Fox" = "CostelloFox", "psymetadata" = "psymetadata",
  "What Works Clearing." = "WWC", "Cochrane" = "Cochrane",
  "Chavalarias et al" = "Chavalarias", "SCORE, all claims" = "SCORE_claims",
  "Lang" = "Lang", "Szucs and Ioannidis" = "Szucs",
  "clinicaltrials.gov + EU CTR" = "ctgov_euctr",
  "Barnett and Wren" = "BarnettWren", "SCORE replications" = "SCORE_replications",
  "OpenSciCollab replications" = "OSC")
# Numeric table rows have a corpus name followed by the estimate of omega.
read_paper_table <- function(path, columns) {
  rows <- grep(" & [0-9]", readLines(path), value = TRUE)
  read_delim(paste(rows, collapse = "\n"), delim = "&", trim_ws = TRUE,
             col_names = c("corpus", columns), col_types = cols(.default = "c")) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(columns), parse_number),
           dataset = unname(table_keys[corpus]))
}
results <- read_paper_table(file.path(bear_root, "paper/tables/table2.tex"),
  c("omega", "signif", "assurance", "replication", "repl_196", "repl_signif",
    "sign", "sign_196", "sign_signif")) %>%
  left_join(read_paper_table(file.path(bear_root, "paper/tables/table3.tex"),
    c("omega", "signif", "assurance", "pos80", "pos80_196", "pos80_signif")) %>%
      select(dataset, pos80), by = "dataset") %>%
  mutate(group = paper_dataset_group(dataset),
         label = unname(slide_labels[dataset]))
stopifnot(nrow(results) == 16, !anyNA(results))
selection_results <- results %>%
  filter(!dataset %in% c("SCORE_replications", "OSC"))
mixtures <- setNames(lapply(paper_selected_datasets, function(d) {
  readRDS(file.path(bear_root, "mixtures", paste0(d, ".rds")))
}), paper_selected_datasets)

# Format ranges from the current tables at their published precision.
percent_range <- function(x) {
  paste0(round(100 * min(x)), "–", round(100 * max(x)), "%")
}
results_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 15, base_family = plot_font) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#E6E7E9", linewidth = 0.3),
        legend.title = element_blank(), legend.position = "top",
        plot.margin = margin(6, 15, 6, 6))
```

:::::::::::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}

```{r selection-estimates, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4.4, out.width='100%'}
selection_results %>% mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(omega, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#999999") +
  geom_point(colour = "#174C70", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(omega)), y = NULL) + results_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13))
```

:::
::: {.column width="51%"}

\small

$\hat\omega$ ranges from **`r min(selection_results$omega)` to `r max(selection_results$omega)`**.

- Many studies have multiple outcomes; we do not know which drive
  publication decisions.
- Hedges' single-parameter model is useful for **adjusting** the distributions
  of $z$-statistics.
- It seems too limited for reliably quantifying and comparing the extent of
  publication bias across fields.

:::
::::::::::::::

\slidesource{Paper Table 2. Replication datasets removed ($\omega=1$ under no selection).}

## Distribution of the probability of significance

:::::::::::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r pos-survival, fig.width=6.3, fig.height=4.3, out.width='100%'}
# Same simulation and survival-curve construction as plot_figure_pos_gap.R.
set.seed(42)
power_curves <- map_dfr(names(mixtures), function(d) {
  fit <- mixtures[[d]]
  snr <- rmix(1e5, p = fit$p, m = fit$m, s = fit$sigma_SNR)
  power <- pnorm(-1.96, snr, 1) + 1 - pnorm(1.96, snr, 1)
  value <- seq(0.05, 1, length.out = 250)
  tibble(dataset = d, value, survival = 1 - ecdf(power)(value))
})
ggplot(power_curves, aes(value, survival, group = dataset)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#777777") +
  geom_line(colour = "#174C70", alpha = 0.55, linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.05, 1), breaks = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.8, 1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = "PoS", y = "Proportion of studies achieving") + results_theme
```

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

\small

\vspace{0.25cm}

Estimated assurance: **`r percent_range(results$assurance)`**.

Only **`r percent_range(results$pos80)`** of studies achieve 80% PoS.

\vspace{0.25cm}

This does not tell us if studies are too small! PoS is "power",
but what matters is power to detect a meaningful effect.

:::
::::::::::::::

\slidesource{Each curve represents a corpus. Paper Tables 2–3; adapted from the PoS figure. Senn (2002).}

## Correct sign versus successful replication

:::::::::::::: {.columns align="top"}
::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r sign-replication, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=4.9, out.width='100%', fig.align='default'}
z_grid <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 5, by = 0.05), 1.96)))
conditional_curves <- map_dfr(names(mixtures), function(d) {
  fit <- mixtures[[d]]
  pr <- gap_vec(z_grid, p = fit$p, m = fit$m, s_snr = fit$sigma_SNR)
  tibble(dataset = d, z = z_grid, `Correct sign` = pr$sgn,
         `Successful replication` = pr$rep)
}) %>% pivot_longer(c(`Correct sign`, `Successful replication`),
                    names_to = "quantity", values_to = "probability")
ggplot(conditional_curves,
       aes(z, probability, group = interaction(dataset, quantity),
           colour = quantity)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.96, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#777777") +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.65, linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Correct sign" = "#174C70",
                                 "Successful replication" = "#858B91")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 5), breaks = c(0, 1.96, 3, 4, 5),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  labs(x = expression(abs(z)), y = "Conditional probability") +
  results_theme + theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.margin = margin(0, 15, 0, 6), legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))
```

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

\small

Unconditionally:

- **`r percent_range(results$sign)`** probability of the correct sign.
- **`r percent_range(results$replication)`** probability of "successful replication".

\vspace{0.3cm}

At $|z|=1.96$:

- **`r percent_range(results$sign_196)`** probability of the correct sign.
- **`r percent_range(results$repl_196)`** probability of "successful replication".

:::
::::::::::::::

\slidesource{Paper Table 2 and conditional-probability figure. Replication has exactly the same SNR and independent sampling error.}

## Marginal significance and the base rate of replication

\small

If $|z|=1.96$, the probability of "successful replication" is never much more
than the base rate, and often even less.

```{r replication-comparison, results='asis'}
results %>% filter(dataset %in% c("Nuijten", "Askarov", "Chavalarias", "Cochrane")) %>%
  transmute(Corpus = label,
            `Randomly selected study` = sprintf("%.0f\\%%", 100 * replication),
            `Conditional on $|z|=1.96$` = sprintf("%.0f\\%%", 100 * repl_196)) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE,
        align = "lrr", linesep = "")
```

- This phenomenon is **not a consequence of many studies having low SNRs**
  (low PoS).
- If all the studies had higher SNRs, the assurance would be higher, but
  observing $|z|=1.96$ would be even less impressive.

\vfill
\slidesource{Paper Table 2. Both columns report the probability of a significant, same-direction exact replication.}

## Results summary

- The estimated distributions generally track the histograms well.
- The main difference between the distributions of the $z$-values is their
  widths; discontinuities at $|z|=1.96$ are a feature of the selection model.
- Estimated assurances range from **`r percent_range(results$assurance)`**;
  **`r percent_range(results$pos80)`** of studies achieve 80% PoS.
- For a marginally significant result, the probability of "successful
  replication" is **`r percent_range(results$repl_196)`**.
- The probability that the direction of the observed effect is correct is
  **`r percent_range(results$sign_196)`**.

\vfill
\slidesource{Paper Tables 2–3. The last two statements condition on $|z|=1.96$.}

## Four features of the empirical corpora

\small

1. **Absolute $z$-values have a decreasing density.**  
   Studies with low SNRs are more common than those with high SNRs.
   Research domains differ considerably in the widths of these distributions.

2. **The probability of significance tends to be low.**  
   Only `r percent_range(results$pos80)` of studies achieve 80% power.

3. **Reaching statistical significance does not imply a high probability
   of replication.**  
   At $|z|=1.96$, the probability of successful replication is
   `r percent_range(results$repl_196)`.

4. **Statistical significance does imply that the sign is likely correct.**  
   At $|z|=1.96$, the probability of the correct sign is
   `r percent_range(results$sign_196)`.

\vfill

## Interpretation: qualified scientific optimism

- Our model allows the PoS to range continuously from 0.05 to 1.
  We observe no clear separation between "true relationships" and
  "no relationships".
- Empirical research often leads to true findings---in the sense of correctly
  identifying the direction of an effect---that do not replicate in the sense
  of achieving statistical significance in the same direction.
- Failure to replicate should not be taken to mean that the original result
  was a fluke or a fake.

\vspace{0.25cm}

**Our qualified optimism extends only to research for which we do not have
decisive reasons to distrust.**


## Which metascience claims survive the empirical data?

\small

*An opinionated summary*

**Supported by this analysis**

- Significant results often fail to replicate significantly.
- Most studies have modest true PoS; only `r percent_range(results$pos80)`
  achieve 80% power. This alone does not establish poor study planning.

**Need qualification or reframing**

- "Most published results are false"; some fields are bad and others
  "gold standard".
- Lowering the $p$-value threshold or uniformly doubling sample sizes
  does not follow from these results.

**Not answered by this paper**

- How common publication bias and $p$-hacking are.
- How much research funding should go to replication.
